Follow one oncogene and its drug through four databases: the mutation in tumours,
the protein, the drug bound to it, and the trial that tested it. **ELO 9.**

Builds on [cancer](../cancer/lec.qmd), [cell death beyond apoptosis](../regulated-necrosis/lec.qmd),
the [disease casebook](../disease-casebook/lec.qmd) and the
[drug journey](../drug-journey/lec.qmd). About 2 hours.

## Part A: in the browser

### A1. The hotspot in melanoma

Open the [BRAF and TP53 mutations in TCGA melanoma](https://www.cbioportal.org/results/mutations?cancer_study_list=skcm_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018&case_set_id=skcm_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018_all&gene_list=BRAF%20TP53)
in cBioPortal. The **Mutations** tab opens with **BRAF** selected. Each lollipop is
one amino-acid position; its height is the number of patients with a mutation there.
Then click **TP53** and compare.

**T1.** At which amino-acid position does BRAF have by far the tallest lollipop? `[ELO 9]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer (checked 2026-11-19)"}
**Position 600** (valine 600, label "V600E/K/R"). Most of these are **V600E**.
TP53, in contrast, has many short lollipops spread over the protein.
:::

### A2. Where is V600 in the protein?

Open [BRAF, UniProt P15056](https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P15056/entry) and go to
the section **Family & Domains**.

**T2.** Which domain contains residue 600? `[ELO 9]`

a. The Ras-binding domain (RBD)
b. The phorbol-ester/DAG-type zinc finger
c. The protein kinase domain

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer (checked 2026-11-19)"}
**c.** The protein kinase domain covers residues 457–717. V600E sits in the
activation segment of the kinase and keeps BRAF active without RAS, so the
RAF–MEK–ERK pathway from the signalling lecture stays on.
:::

### A3. The drug in the binding site

Open [PDB 3OG7](https://www.rcsb.org/structure/3OG7), "B-Raf Kinase V600E oncogenic
mutant in complex with PLX4032". PLX4032 is the development name of vemurafenib.
Scroll to **Small Molecules**.

**T3.** What is the three-character ligand ID of vemurafenib? `[ELO 9]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer (checked 2026-11-19)"}
**032.** The structure contains only the kinase domain, with the V600E mutation:
the drug binds the ATP pocket of the mutant kinase.
:::

### A4. The trial

Open the BRIM-3 trial, [NCT01006980](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT01006980),
and look at **Arms and Interventions**.

**T4.** Which drug was vemurafenib compared with? `[ELO 9]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer (checked 2026-11-19)"}
**Dacarbazine**, a standard chemotherapy. Only patients whose melanoma carried
**BRAF V600E** could join: the drug is aimed at the mutant protein.
You meet trial design again in *Kliniska prövningar och läkemedelsutveckling*.
:::

## Part B: in R

Install the packages once in the console:

```r
install.packages(c("rmarkdown", "ggplot2", "jsonlite"))
```

Download the template and the data snapshot. Put the template in a new folder and the
CSV in a subfolder `data/`.

- [R Markdown template](bioinfo-cancer-genomics.Rmd)
- [Snapshot: BRAF and TP53 mutations](data/skcm-mutations-2026-11-18.csv)

Data: cBioPortal, TCGA Skin Cutaneous Melanoma PanCancer Atlas (public TCGA data), retrieved 2026-11-18.

The **Data** chunk is complete: it reads all BRAF and TP53 mutations from the
cBioPortal API into a table `mutations` with one row per mutation. If cBioPortal is
down, it reads the snapshot instead (or set `use_snapshot <- TRUE`). Your job is to
build the steps after it: **read → filter → plot**. Fill the three blanks `___`
and knit.

1. **Chunk `lollipop`:** put the column with the amino-acid position on the x axis.
   You should see two panels, like Part A, made from your own data.
2. **Chunk `position-600`:** build a pipeline from the three given pieces, in the
   right order, joined by `|>`. It starts with the data, keeps only BRAF position 600,
   then counts each protein change. It prints a small table of changes.
3. **Chunk `mutation-types`:** colour the bars by the column that holds the
   mutation type (look at the column names printed by the Data chunk, or run
   `names(mutations)`). You should see one stacked bar per gene.

**T5.** In your lollipop plot, compare the tallest BRAF lollipop with the tallest TP53 lollipop. `[ELO 9]`

a. They are about the same height
b. BRAF's is about 5 times taller
c. BRAF's is about 30 times taller

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer (checked 2026-11-19)"}
**c.** BRAF position 600 has 198 mutations; the tallest TP53 position (213) has 7.
One position dominates BRAF; TP53 mutations are scattered.
:::

**T6.** Your `position_600` table: which change is the second most common at BRAF position 600? `[ELO 9]`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer (checked 2026-11-19)"}
**V600K** (35 mutations, after 158 V600E). Both replace valine 600 and both activate the kinase.
:::

**T7. [VG]** Your mutation-type plot: which statement fits? `[ELO 9]`

a. Both genes have mostly missense mutations, so both are oncogenes
b. TP53 has many nonsense, frameshift and splice mutations that cut the protein short;
   BRAF has almost only missense mutations
c. BRAF has more nonsense mutations than TP53

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer (checked 2026-11-19)"}
**b.** BRAF: 241 of 245 are missense. TP53: 23 nonsense, 3 frameshift and 7 splice-site
mutations among 82. An oncogene needs one precise change that turns it **on**, so the
same position is hit again and again. A tumour suppressor is turned **off**, and many
different changes do that, including stopping the protein early. This is why a
drug can block BRAF V600E, but no pill can bring back a lost p53.
:::

## Hand in

- The knitted HTML, with no error messages.
- The two plots and the `position_600` table.
- Your answers to T5–T7, one line each, in the **Answers** section of the template.
